courses.name: Personal & Professional Development

content.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
content.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
content.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
content.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.contribution: Required first-year academic/reflective formation; specific academic writing/presentation correspondence separately reviewed.

courses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies

content.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
content.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication

content.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
content.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.

content.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

courses.name: Modern History

content.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
content.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.

courses.name: Native American Histories

content.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
content.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
content.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
content.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production

concept.label: Literature, rhetoric & cultural history
concept.concept: Study literary form, linguistic stylistics, rhetoric and film alongside American cultural representation and source-based history. Social theory and the philosophy of emotion support focused analyses of identity, power and artistic response; a dedicated English-proficiency curriculum, structural and historical linguistics sequence, and the full British literary-period sequence remain gaps.
concept.labelReason: Six literature, four communication, five media and five history courses form the main curriculum; two sociology courses and Philosophy of Emotion supply specific complementary interpretation. The descriptive label fits this sustained literary/cultural response without promising the full English Studies discipline.
progression: All exact workbook terms and formal prerequisites pass. Literary introduction and stylistics precede advanced literary research; rhetoric precedes its practice module; film introduction precedes documentary and adaptation; introductory sociology precedes Modern Sociology; modern history precedes the source-based seminar. Level-three Philosophy of Emotion has no formal prerequisite and is placed in the final semester.

candidateChallenge: One coherent related-fields response materially addresses literary interpretation, linguistic stylistics, cultural production and representation, with 6 literature, 4 communication, 5 media and 5 history courses; it is not merely general humanities breadth. Literature/culture is already substantively covered and gives no second distinct concept. The first additional structural/historical/global English-linguistics direction was tested against Style & Meaning (actual syntax, semantics, discourse, pragmatics and cognition) and Psycholinguistics (acquisition, bilingualism, speech processing and hands-on experiments), brain/behaviour foundations and research methods. These are positive contributions, but cannot supply a coherent 24-course response to English structure, variation, phonology and historical development; generic psychology or computing substitutions would change its defining subject. Advanced proficiency lacks a dedicated development sequence despite genuine rhetorical, academic and creative writing. Science/politics/business describes English-language use, not three curricular specializations. Teaching was tested through primary-school rhetorical teaching, Psycholinguistics, brain/behaviour and Lifespan Developmental Psychology; these do not establish an English-learning/secondary pedagogy programme. Rejection is substantive, not the lack of a teaching licence. Stop after the first failed additional concept; subsequent retained tests document coverage, not a third alternative.
